lessons.title: Calculus: Differentiation
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Understand the concept of a derivative
Apply differentiation to find gradients and turning points
lessons.reading_material: Calculus was invented by Newton and Leibniz and revolutionised science. DIFFERENTIATION finds the rate of change (gradient) of a function at any point. For f(x)=xⁿ, the derivative f'(x)=nxⁿ⁻¹. Example: f(x)=x³, f'(x)=3x². At a MAXIMUM or MINIMUM, f'(x)=0. Second derivative tells us if it's a max or min. Used in physics, economics, engineering, and science!
practical_activities: Gradient of curves investigation
Optimisation problems (maximum area)
Velocity from position function

homework.task: Find the turning points of f(x)=x³−3x²+2. Determine if each is a max or min.

revision.notes: Power rule: d/dx(xⁿ)=nxⁿ⁻¹. Sum rule: differentiate each term. Turning points: set f'(x)=0. Second derivative test.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: If f'(x)=0 and f''(x)<0, the point is a?

lessons.title: Calculus: Integration
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: INTEGRATION is the reverse of differentiation — and also calculates areas under curves. For ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (C = constant of integration). DEFINITE INTEGRALS calculate exact area: ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a). Example: ∫[1 to 3] x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3. This is the foundation of physics, engineering, and economics.
practical_activities: Area estimation using rectangles then integration
Velocity to displacement problems
Economic surplus calculation

homework.task: Find the area under y=x²+1 between x=0 and x=3 using integration. Sketch the region.

revision.notes: Integration: ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C. Definite: [F(x)] from a to b = F(b)−F(a). Area = definite integral.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Statistics: Regression and Correlation
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: CORRELATION measures how strongly two variables are related. Pearson's r: −1 (perfect negative), 0 (no correlation), +1 (perfect positive). REGRESSION finds the equation of the best-fit line: ŷ = mx + c. Used to PREDICT values. Example: exam score predicted from hours studied. CAUSATION ≠ CORRELATION — a relationship doesn't mean one causes the other!
practical_activities: Scatter graph with class data (height/shoe size)
Calculate correlation coefficient
Regression line for prediction

exercises.q: If regression line is y=2x+5, predict y when x=8.

homework.task: Collect paired data (e.g. study hours and test scores) for 10 students. Plot scatter graph, find r, draw regression line.

revision.notes: r close to ±1: strong correlation. r near 0: weak. Regression: ŷ=a+bx. Predict within range only (extrapolation risky).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Mathematical Proof
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: A MATHEMATICAL PROOF is a logical argument that a statement is always true. Types: DEDUCTIVE proof (using known facts to prove new ones), PROOF BY CONTRADICTION (assume opposite, show it leads to contradiction), PROOF BY INDUCTION (base case + inductive step). A CONJECTURE is a statement we think is true but haven't proved. ONE counter-example disproves any conjecture!
practical_activities: Prove algebraic identities
Prove geometric theorems
Find counter-examples to false conjectures

exercises.q: To disprove a conjecture, you need?
Prove: the sum of two odd numbers is even.
exercises.answer: Let odd numbers be 2m+1 and 2n+1. Sum = 2m+2n+2 = 2(m+n+1) which is even.

homework.task: Prove algebraically: (a+b)² − (a−b)² = 4ab for all values of a and b.

revision.notes: Proof: logical chain from known to new. Counter-example: n=1 suffices to disprove. Contradiction: assume ¬P, derive absurdity.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Extended Writing: Essay Craft
lessons.subject: English
lessons.reading_material: At the highest level, writing is about argument, evidence, and nuance. ACADEMIC ESSAYS require: INTRODUCTION (hook, context, thesis), BODY PARAGRAPHS (PEEL/TEEL, topic sentences, embedded quotations), CONCLUSION (synthesis, not summary). Sophisticated writing uses: varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, hedging language ('arguably', 'it could be suggested'), and acknowledges complexity.
practical_activities: Workshop on essay introductions
Peer critique of essays
Write under timed conditions

exercises.q: Hedging language in academic writing serves to?

exercises.answer: Synthesise the argument, not merely summarise. Return to the thesis with added insight from the essay.

homework.task: Write a 600-word analytical essay: 'Explore how a writer of your choice presents power.' Plan → draft → edit → proofread.

revision.notes: Essay: intro (hook+thesis), body (PEEL×3+), conclusion (synthesis). Vary sentence length. Use 'arguably', 'perhaps', 'one might suggest'.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

options: putting quotation in a separate paragraph
weaving the quotation into your sentence
questions.answer: weaving the quotation into your sentence

options: Synthesis of main ideas returning to thesis with new insight
questions.answer: Synthesis of main ideas returning to thesis with new insight

lessons.title: Language and Power
lessons.subject: English
lessons.reading_material: Language is never neutral — it reflects and constructs power relationships. CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS (CDA) examines how texts reinforce or challenge ideology. Key concepts: FRAMING (how events are presented), LEXICAL CHOICES (word choice), PRESUPPOSITION (assumptions built into language), DISCOURSE COMMUNITY. Media representations of gender, race, class, and politics reveal social power structures.
practical_activities: Analyse political speeches for power language
Deconstruct advertising for hidden messages
Write a CDA of a news report

options: choosing what to include and how to present it
exercises.answer: choosing what to include and how to present it

homework.task: Choose a political speech. Analyse: 1) Who holds power? 2) What framing is used? 3) What is assumed? 4) Whose voices are absent?

revision.notes: Language shapes reality. Presupposition: questions that assume things ('Have you stopped cheating?' assumes you were). Always ask: who benefits from this framing?
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

options: an assumption built into a statement
questions.answer: an assumption built into a statement

lessons.title: Ecology and Ecosystems
lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Define ecosystem and describe its components
Analyse the impact of human activity on ecosystems
lessons.reading_material: An ecosystem includes all living organisms and their non-living environment. Biotic factors = living (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria). Abiotic factors = non-living (water, temperature, soil, light). Human activities (deforestation, pollution) disrupt ecosystems. Conservation and sustainability are responses.
practical_activities: Map a local ecosystem (schoolyard)
Debate: logging vs conservation

homework.task: Research one endangered ecosystem and the threats it faces

revision.notes: Abiotic = non-living. Biotic = living. Both interact to form ecosystem.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Quantum Theory and Relativity (Introduction)
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Classical physics breaks down at atomic scales. Quantum theory states energy comes in discrete packets called quanta (photons for light). Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: we cannot know position and momentum simultaneously. Einstein's special relativity: E=mc², time dilation, mass-energy equivalence. These theories underpin modern technology (MRI, transistors, GPS).
practical_activities: Research: how does a transistor use quantum mechanics?
Calculate mass-energy using E=mc² for a small mass

options: Energy = mass × speed of light squared
exercises.answer: Energy = mass × speed of light squared

homework.task: Write a paragraph explaining one application of quantum theory

revision.notes: Quantum theory and relativity together explain the universe at small and large scales.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Globalisation and Its Impacts
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Evaluate positive and negative effects of globalisation
Analyse the role of TNCs in development
lessons.reading_material: Globalisation integrates economies, cultures, and politics. Transnational corporations (TNCs) operate globally — they bring jobs and investment but may exploit cheap labour and cause environmental damage. Cultural globalisation spreads ideas and brands but risks cultural homogenisation. Contested: is globalisation reducing or increasing inequality?
practical_activities: Case study: Samsung or Nike — TNC and its global impact
Debate: is globalisation good for developing countries?

options: A company operating in multiple countries
exercises.answer: A company operating in multiple countries

homework.task: Research one TNC and analyse its economic and social impact in a developing country

revision.notes: TNCs bring investment but can exploit workers and damage environment. Globalisation is contested.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Sustainability and the Future
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Evaluate the SDGs and their progress
lessons.reading_material: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland 1987). The UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) target poverty, education, health, equality, climate, and ecosystems by 2030. Progress is uneven. Local, national, and global action is required.
practical_activities: Evaluate progress on 3 SDGs using data
Design a local sustainability project

homework.task: Choose one SDG and research your country's progress toward it

revision.notes: SDGs = 17 global goals for 2030. Sustainability = meeting needs without harming the future.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: 20th Century: Ideologies and Conflicts
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Compare fascism, communism, and liberal democracy
Analyse how ideology shaped 20th century conflicts
lessons.reading_material: The 20th century was shaped by competing ideologies. Fascism (Italy, Germany): ultranationalism, authoritarianism, racism. Communism (USSR, China, Cuba): state ownership, classless society. Liberal democracy (USA, UK): individual rights, free markets. These ideologies fuelled WWI, WWII, Cold War, and decolonisation. Lessons: unchecked ideology leads to atrocity.
practical_activities: Compare Hitler, Stalin, and Churchill's worldviews
Analyse how propaganda shaped belief in Nazi Germany

exercises.q: Which ideology emphasises state control of the economy and classless society?

homework.task: Write a comparative analysis: how did different ideologies lead to WWII?

revision.notes: Fascism=nationalist+authoritarian. Communism=statist+classless. Democracy=individual rights+free market.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: The World Since 1991
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Analyse major global events since the Cold War
lessons.reading_material: Since 1991: US hegemony, 9/11 and War on Terror, rise of China, Arab Spring, climate crisis, COVID-19 pandemic, AI revolution, Ukraine war. Globalisation accelerated but nationalist backlash grew. Challenges: inequality, climate change, democratic backsliding, geopolitical competition. Historians debate: are we in a more or less stable world than during the Cold War?
practical_activities: Timeline of key post-1991 events
Debate: what is the most important challenge of the 21st century?

homework.task: Write an analysis: what do you think will be history's most important question about our current era?

revision.notes: Post-Cold War: US dominance → multipolar world → global challenges (climate, AI, inequality).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Ethics, Justice, and Islam in the Modern World
lessons.subject: Islamic Studies
learning_objectives: Apply Islamic ethical principles to contemporary issues
lessons.reading_material: Islamic ethics centres on maqasid al-shariah (objectives of Islamic law): protection of life, intellect, lineage, wealth, and religion. Scholars engage with modern issues: bioethics (organ donation, IVF), finance (interest-free banking), environment (Islamic ecology), human rights, and gender. Ijtihad (independent reasoning) allows Islamic scholarship to address new questions.
practical_activities: Case study: Islamic finance vs conventional banking
Debate: how does Islam respond to climate change?

homework.task: Research one contemporary issue and find an Islamic scholarly perspective on it

revision.notes: Maqasid = protect life, intellect, lineage, wealth, religion. Ijtihad allows new solutions.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Algorithms and Data Structures
lessons.subject: Coding
lessons.reading_material: Sorting and searching are fundamental problems in computer science. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements to sort a list. Binary search halves the search space each step — much faster than linear search for sorted data.
practical_activities: Implement bubble sort in Python
Compare linear vs binary search on a list of 1000 items
exercises: Trace bubble sort on [5, 3, 8, 1, 2]
Write a Python binary search function
lessons.homework: Research and implement one other sorting algorithm (selection sort or insertion sort).

revision.notes: Big O notation describes how runtime grows with input size. O(n²) < O(n log n) < O(n) < O(log n) in efficiency.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.assessment: Implement both bubble sort and binary search in Python and test with at least 10 elements.

lessons.title: Nobel Literature — Global Voices
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Analyse works of Nobel Literature laureates
lessons.reading_material: The Nobel Prize in Literature recognises the world's greatest writers. Recent laureates: Olga Tokarczuk (Poland, 2018) — 'Flights' weaves short narratives into a meditation on movement. Peter Handke (Austria, 2019) — controversial for political positions; his plays challenge theatrical convention. Abdulrazak Gurnah (Tanzania/UK, 2021) — novels about East African refugees and colonialism. Annie Ernaux (France, 2022) — autofiction about class, gender, and memory. Mo Yan (China, 2012) — magic realism depicting modern Chinese history. Literary analysis: close reading, intertextuality, author's craft, cultural context.
practical_activities: Close reading workshop: analyse one paragraph from a Nobel laureate text — discuss every word choice
exercises: What is autofiction? Give an example
Name 3 Nobel Prize winners from non-Western countries
Explain intertextuality with an example from two texts
lessons.homework: Read the Nobel Prize lecture of any laureate — summarise their main ideas about literature in 200 words.

revision.notes: Nobel laureates represent world literary diversity. Close reading = analysis of language, structure, and meaning.
revision.tip: Nobel lectures are brilliant — laureates explain their whole literary philosophy in one speech.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Boulevard des Capucines
info_cards.fact: "The Boulevard des Capucines" by Claude Monet. An Impressionist view of a bustling Paris street from above.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Woman with a Parasol
info_cards.fact: "Woman with a Parasol" by Claude Monet. Shows Monet's wife and son walking in a field on a breezy day.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Magpie
info_cards.fact: "The Magpie" by Claude Monet. A snowy landscape painting featuring a small magpie perched on a gate.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Rouen Cathedral
info_cards.fact: "Rouen Cathedral" by Claude Monet. Part of a series of paintings Monet made of the same cathedral facade in different light.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Haystacks
info_cards.fact: "Haystacks" by Claude Monet. A series of paintings showing haystacks in a field at different times of day.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Japanese Footbridge
info_cards.fact: "The Japanese Footbridge" by Claude Monet. Shows the wooden bridge over the water-lily pond in Monet's garden.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Paris Street; Rainy Day
info_cards.fact: "Paris Street; Rainy Day" by Gustave Caillebotte. A realistic painting of Parisians walking with umbrellas on a wet street.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Floor Scrapers
info_cards.fact: "The Floor Scrapers" by Gustave Caillebotte. Shows workers scraping a wooden floor, a scene of everyday Parisian life.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Dance at Bougival
info_cards.fact: "Dance at Bougival" by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Shows a couple dancing outdoors at a popular riverside dance hall.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
info_cards.fact: "Two Sisters (On the Terrace)" by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. A warm portrait of two young women on a balcony overlooking the Seine.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Paddington Bear Statue
info_cards.fact: "Paddington Bear Statue" by Marcus Cornish. A bronze statue of the beloved storybook bear at Paddington Station, London.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Oliver Twist Statue
info_cards.fact: "Oliver Twist Statue" by Civic sculptors. A public statue honouring Charles Dickens' famous storybook character.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Open University Sundial Sculpture
info_cards.fact: "The Open University Sundial Sculpture" by Civic sculptors. A modern public artwork combining sculpture with a working sundial.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Wall of Fame Sculptures (various cities)
info_cards.fact: "Wall of Fame Sculptures (various cities)" by Various civic sculptors. Decorative public sculptures celebrating community history and achievement.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Awakening of Spring
info_cards.fact: "The Awakening of Spring" by Auguste Rodin (school). A bronze relief sculpture symbolizing renewal and the arrival of springtime.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Cellist (Civic Bronze)
info_cards.fact: "Cellist (Civic Bronze)" by Various civic sculptors. A public bronze statue honouring musicians, found in several city plazas.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Bremen Town Musicians Statue
info_cards.fact: "The Bremen Town Musicians Statue" by Gerhard Marcks. A bronze statue in Bremen, Germany, depicting the animal heroes of the Grimm fairy tale.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Sun Voyager
info_cards.fact: "Sun Voyager" by Jon Gunnar Arnason. A striking steel sculpture shaped like a Viking ship, standing in Reykjavik, Iceland.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Fearless Girl
info_cards.fact: "The Fearless Girl" by Kristen Visbal. A bronze statue of a young girl standing confidently, originally placed near Wall Street.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Spirit of Detroit
info_cards.fact: "The Spirit of Detroit" by Marshall Fredericks. A large bronze sculpture in Detroit, Michigan, depicting a seated figure holding symbols of family and community.

lessons.title: Art Criticism and Art History
lessons.subject: Art
learning_objectives: Analyse a work of art using DABLS (Describe, Analyse, Interpret, Judge)
lessons.reading_material: Art criticism uses structured methods to analyse artworks. DABLS: Describe (what you see), Analyse (how it is organised), Interpret (what it means), Evaluate (is it successful and why?). Art history charts the evolution of artistic styles from Renaissance to Contemporary.
practical_activities: Write a formal analysis of a chosen artwork
Present and evaluate your own portfolio piece
exercises: Identify the movement and period of 5 artworks
Write a 300-word DABLS analysis
lessons.homework: Research one art movement and create a 1-minute presentation on its key features and artists.

revision.notes: D-A-B-L-S: Describe → Analyse → Interpret (meaning) → Judge (evaluate). Each step builds on the last.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which step of DABLS asks 'what does it mean?'
Which art movement is known for painting outdoors to capture light?

lessons.assessment: Write a complete DABLS analysis (400+ words) of a significant artwork of your choice.

lessons.title: History of Western Music
lessons.subject: Music
learning_objectives: Identify major periods of Western music history
Name key composers from each period
lessons.reading_material: Western music history: Medieval (chants, sacred), Renaissance (polyphony, madrigals), Baroque (Bach, Handel — ornamentation), Classical (Mozart, Haydn — clarity, balance), Romantic (Beethoven, Chopin — emotion, drama), Modern/Contemporary (Stravinsky, jazz, electronic).
practical_activities: Listen to representative pieces from 3 different periods
Compare how tempo, texture, and instruments differ
exercises: Match composers to their period
Describe 3 differences between Baroque and Romantic music
lessons.homework: Research one composer and prepare a 2-minute biography including their historical period and key works.

revision.notes: Remember: Bach = Baroque. Mozart = Classical. Beethoven bridges Classical and Romantic.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which period features Bach and Handel?
Which period is characterised by emotional expression and large orchestras?

lessons.assessment: Essay: Compare two composers from different periods. How does their music reflect the values of their time?

lessons.title: Mental Resilience in Crisis
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Explain the psychological stages of a crisis
lessons.reading_material: Physical survival is only half the challenge — mental resilience is equally critical. In a crisis, people often go through stages: denial, panic/fear, resistance, and acceptance. Panic wastes energy and impairs decision-making. Strategies for maintaining composure: controlled breathing (box breathing — inhale 4 sec, hold 4 sec, exhale 4 sec, hold 4 sec), positive self-talk, focusing on what you can control, and taking one small action. Post-traumatic growth (PTG) — some people emerge from adversity stronger, more resilient, and with a clearer sense of purpose. Building resilience before a crisis: strong social networks, physical fitness, skills training, and reflection.
practical_activities: Box breathing practice (4-4-4-4 technique) — then discuss: how did it affect your state?
exercises: Name the psychological stages of a crisis
Explain box breathing and when to use it
What is post-traumatic growth?
lessons.homework: Write a personal resilience plan: 3 strategies you will use in a high-stress situation.

revision.notes: Crisis stages: denial → panic → resistance → acceptance. Box breathing calms nervous system. PTG = growing through adversity.
revision.tip: Resilience is a skill, not a personality trait — anyone can build it with practice.

quiz.question: Post-traumatic growth means
options: Growing stronger and wiser through adversity
quiz.correct: Growing stronger and wiser through adversity

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word reflection: What does mental resilience mean to you and how will you build it?
textbook_references: Bear Grylls Survival Guide for Young People
The Resilience Project — Hugh van Cuylenburg

lessons.title: Food Entrepreneurship
lessons.subject: Cooking
lessons.reading_material: Food businesses must satisfy customers, comply with food safety law, and be profitable. Food safety: HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) identifies risks at each production stage. Legal requirements: food hygiene certificate, premises registration, allergen labelling (14 major allergens must be declared). Profit margin = (Revenue − Costs) ÷ Revenue × 100. USP (Unique Selling Point) differentiates a product in a crowded market. Start-up costs include equipment, rent, ingredients, and marketing.
practical_activities: Develop a business plan for a food product: concept, costings, target market, USP, pricing
exercises: Define HACCP and explain one critical control point
Calculate profit margin if revenue=$500 and costs=$320
Name 5 of the 14 major allergens that must be labelled
lessons.homework: Research the food hygiene rating system in your country and what businesses need to achieve the top rating.

revision.notes: HACCP = food safety system. 14 allergens must be labelled. Profit margin = (Revenue−Costs)÷Revenue×100%.
revision.tip: A high profit margin means more sustainable business — keep costs low and value high.

quiz.question: HACCP stands for
options: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points
quiz.correct: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points

lessons.assessment: Write a 2-page food business plan including concept, costings, USP, and food safety considerations.

lessons.title: Advanced Arabic — Debate and Persuasion
lessons.subject: Foreign Languages
learning_objectives: Construct a persuasive argument in Arabic
lessons.reading_material: Persuasive Arabic uses specific rhetorical strategies: استفهام إنكاري (rhetorical question), تكرار (repetition for emphasis), مبالغة (hyperbole), and statistical evidence. A persuasive speech structure: hook (استهلال), thesis (أطروحة), arguments (حجج), counter-argument (رد على الحجج المعارضة), conclusion (خاتمة). Famous Arabic speeches include those of Gamal Abdel Nasser and President Erdoğan's UN speeches in Arabic. Advanced Arabic requires command of case endings, subjunctive mood, and complex nominal sentences.
practical_activities: Formal Arabic debate: two teams argue a motion in MSA — judged on language and argument quality
exercises: Write a 250-word persuasive essay in Arabic on 'Should mobile phones be allowed in schools?'
Identify two rhetorical devices in a given Arabic speech excerpt
Write and deliver a 90-second persuasive speech in Arabic
lessons.homework: Research an Arabic speech by a famous leader — identify at least two rhetorical devices.

revision.notes: Persuasion = استهلال + أطروحة + حجج + رد + خاتمة. Use rhetorical questions and repetition.
revision.tip: Practise speaking aloud — Arabic rhetoric is meant to be heard, not just read.

lessons.assessment: Deliver a 2-minute persuasive speech in Arabic and respond to one question from the audience.

info_cards.title: Famous Places
info_cards.fact: The Great Wall of China is not a single continuous wall but a network of walls and fortifications built over many centuries by different dynasties.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "I think, therefore I am." — Rene Descartes.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "The unexamined life is not worth living." — Socrates.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Marie Curie
info_cards.fact: Marie Curie was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry), for her research on radioactivity.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: A Brief History of Time
info_cards.fact: Stephen Hawking's "A Brief History of Time" explains complex ideas about the origin and nature of the universe, including black holes and the Big Bang, for a general audience.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Guns, Germs, and Steel
info_cards.fact: "Guns, Germs, and Steel" by Jared Diamond examines how geography, agriculture, and disease shaped the rise of different societies throughout history.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Malala Yousafzai
info_cards.fact: "One child, one teacher, one book, one pen can change the world." — Pakistani activist for girls' education who became the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Greta Thunberg
info_cards.fact: "You are never too small to make a difference." — Swedish climate activist who began a global youth movement for climate action with her school strikes.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Barack Obama
info_cards.fact: "Change will not come if we wait for some other person or some other time. We are the ones we've been waiting for." — 44th U.S. president and the first African American to hold the office.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Angela Merkel
info_cards.fact: "We can do this." — German chancellor who led Germany for sixteen years and played a central role in European politics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Kofi Annan
info_cards.fact: "Knowledge is power. Information is liberating." — Ghanaian diplomat who served as Secretary-General of the United Nations and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jacinda Ardern
info_cards.fact: "One of the things I'd like to think is people give a bit more credit to... kindness with strength." — New Zealand prime minister known for her crisis leadership and communication style.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Malcolm X
info_cards.fact: "Education is the passport to the future, for tomorrow belongs to those who prepare for it today." — American minister and human-rights activist who advocated for Black empowerment and self-determination.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Cesar Chavez
info_cards.fact: "We cannot seek achievement for ourselves and forget about progress and prosperity for our community." — American labor leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to advocate for farmworkers' rights.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Dolores Huerta
info_cards.fact: "Every moment is an organizing opportunity, every person a potential activist, every minute a chance to change the world." — American labor leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers union alongside Cesar Chavez.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Marie Marvingt
info_cards.fact: "Above all, do not give up." — French aviator and athlete known as 'the fiancée of danger' for her pioneering work in aviation and medicine.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Sally Ride
info_cards.fact: "I would like to be remembered as someone who was not afraid to do what she wanted to do." — American astronaut who became the first American woman in space in 1983.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mae Jemison
info_cards.fact: "Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations." — American engineer and astronaut who became the first African American woman to travel into space.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Yuri Gagarin
info_cards.fact: "I see the Earth! It is so beautiful." — Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into outer space in 1961.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Valentina Tereshkova
info_cards.fact: "Once you've been in space, you appreciate how small and fragile this planet is." — Soviet cosmonaut who became the first woman in space in 1963.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Sundar Pichai
info_cards.fact: "Wear your failure as a badge of honor." — Indian-American businessman who serves as CEO of Google and its parent company, Alphabet.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Tu Youyou
info_cards.fact: "I love my work and there is nothing in the world I'd rather do." — Chinese pharmaceutical chemist who discovered artemisinin, a life-saving treatment for malaria, winning the Nobel Prize.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Frances Arnold
info_cards.fact: "You can use evolution to design new molecules... that solve today's problems." — American chemical engineer who won the Nobel Prize for pioneering directed evolution of enzymes.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Tawakkol Karman
info_cards.fact: "Peace cannot be achieved without women's full participation." — Yemeni journalist and activist who won the Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting women's rights and democracy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Denis Mukwege
info_cards.fact: "Healing is a journey... it requires us all." — Congolese gynecologist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate known for his work treating survivors of sexual violence.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Abiy Ahmed
info_cards.fact: "We can either make the most of the rich, ample resources we have, or squander them." — Ethiopian prime minister who won the Nobel Peace Prize for ending a long conflict with neighboring Eritrea.

lessons.title: Global Citizenship and Future Challenges
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
learning_objectives: Propose personal contributions to global solutions
lessons.reading_material: A global citizen understands their rights and responsibilities in an interconnected world. Future challenges include: climate change accelerating, growing inequality between rich and poor nations, resource scarcity (water, food, energy), rise of misinformation, and geopolitical tensions over technology dominance. Global citizenship requires empathy, critical thinking, intercultural competence, and a commitment to sustainability. Every individual — regardless of age or nationality — can contribute through informed choices, advocacy, and community action.
practical_activities: Action project: choose one global challenge and design a small-scale response for your school community
exercises: Define global citizenship in your own words
Name three future challenges and explain their causes
How can a student act as a global citizen without leaving their city?
lessons.homework: Write a letter to a world leader proposing one policy to address a global challenge you care about.

revision.notes: Global citizen = informed, empathetic, active participant in solving shared problems.
revision.tip: Think globally, act locally — change starts in your own community.

quiz.question: Which of these is a characteristic of a global citizen?
options: Only caring about their own country
Being informed and empathetic about global issues
quiz.correct: Being informed and empathetic about global issues

quiz.question: Resource scarcity refers to
options: Running out of essential resources like water and food
quiz.correct: Running out of essential resources like water and food

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word personal commitment statement: what will you do as a global citizen over the next year?

lessons.title: Political Ideologies
lessons.subject: Social Studies
learning_objectives: Compare their views on government, economy, and society
lessons.reading_material: Political ideologies are sets of ideas about how society should be organised. Liberalism: individual freedoms, democracy, rule of law, market economy. Conservatism: tradition, social stability, gradual change. Socialism: equality, collective ownership, welfare state. Nationalism: prioritising national identity and interests. Environmentalism: sustainability and ecological limits on economic growth. In reality, most political parties mix elements of several ideologies. Understanding ideologies helps citizens evaluate political arguments and vote wisely.
practical_activities: Political spectrum mapping: place given policies on a left-right political spectrum — class discussion
exercises: Define liberalism and conservatism and explain one difference
Where does environmentalism fit on the traditional left-right spectrum?
Why do most political parties combine several ideologies?
lessons.homework: Analyse the manifesto of a political party in your country — identify its main ideological elements.

revision.notes: Key ideologies: Liberalism (freedom), Conservatism (tradition), Socialism (equality), Nationalism (nation), Environmentalism (ecology).
revision.tip: No ideology has all the answers — critical evaluation is essential.

quiz.question: Which ideology prioritises environmental sustainability above economic growth?

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word analysis comparing TWO political ideologies on one specific issue (e.g. taxation).

lessons.title: Sustainable Development
lessons.subject: Environmental Science
learning_objectives: Analyse trade-offs between development and environment
lessons.reading_material: Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising future generations. The UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) address poverty, hunger, health, education, climate, and more. Real sustainability balances economic, social, and environmental needs.
practical_activities: Map which SDGs are most relevant to your community
Design a sustainable community plan
exercises: Identify 3 trade-offs in a development scenario
Explain the difference between a linear and circular economy
lessons.homework: Research how one country is implementing a specific SDG and evaluate its progress.

revision.notes: The 3 pillars of sustainability: People (social), Planet (environment), Profit (economic).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What does sustainable development mean?
options: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations
questions.correct: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations

questions.question: How many UN Sustainable Development Goals are there?

lessons.assessment: Essay: Evaluate the tension between economic development and environmental protection using a real case study.

lessons.title: Macroeconomics — GDP, Inflation, Unemployment
lessons.subject: Economics
learning_objectives: Explain causes and effects of inflation
Analyse the relationship between inflation and unemployment
lessons.reading_material: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measures total output of an economy. GDP = C + I + G + (X−M) (Consumption + Investment + Government spending + Net exports). Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Causes: demand-pull (excess demand), cost-push (rising production costs). The Phillips Curve (historically) suggested an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment. Central banks use interest rates to control inflation.
practical_activities: Calculate GDP from given data; plot an inflation vs unemployment graph and interpret
exercises: Calculate GDP from data: C=500, I=200, G=300, X=100, M=80
Distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation
What does the Phillips Curve show?
lessons.homework: Find your country's current GDP and inflation rate from a central bank website — compare to last year.

revision.notes: GDP = C+I+G+(X−M). Inflation measured by CPI. Phillips Curve: low unemployment → higher inflation.
revision.tip: Know the GDP formula — it appears in almost every macroeconomics exam.

quiz.question: Cost-push inflation is caused by
options: Too much money in the economy

lessons.assessment: Given macroeconomic data for a country, identify economic challenges and propose TWO policy responses.

lessons.title: Investing and Financial Planning
lessons.subject: Finance
learning_objectives: Differentiate types of investment (stocks, bonds, property)
Create a basic long-term financial plan
lessons.reading_material: Investing grows wealth over time. Stocks (shares): buying part ownership of a company — higher risk, higher potential return. Bonds: lending money to a company or government — lower risk, fixed return. Property: real estate — tangible asset, illiquid. Diversification reduces risk by spreading investments across different assets. Index funds track market averages and are low-cost. A financial plan sets goals (retirement, education, home purchase) and maps steps to achieve them.
practical_activities: Build a mock portfolio: allocate £10,000 across stocks, bonds, and property — justify your choices
exercises: Explain the difference between a stock and a bond
Why is diversification important?
Create a 10-year financial goal and outline three steps to achieve it
lessons.homework: Research the performance of any stock market index over the last 10 years — what pattern do you see?

revision.notes: Stocks = ownership + high risk. Bonds = lending + low risk. Diversify to reduce risk. Plan early!
revision.tip: Time in the market beats timing the market — invest consistently, don't try to predict peaks.

quiz.question: An index fund
options: Tracks a market index with low fees
quiz.correct: Tracks a market index with low fees

lessons.assessment: Design a 10-year investment plan with goals, asset allocation, and projected growth.

lessons.title: Advanced First Aid — Burns, Fractures, Anaphylaxis
lessons.subject: First Aid
lessons.reading_material: Burns: cool with running water for 20 minutes, do NOT use ice or butter, cover with cling film or a clean bag, call 999. Fractures: do not move the casualty unless in danger, support the limb in position found, use improvised splints. Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction): signs = swelling of throat/tongue, difficulty breathing, rash, low blood pressure. Treatment: lay flat (or sit up if breathing difficulty), administer adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) into outer thigh, call 999, give second EpiPen after 5 minutes if no improvement.
practical_activities: Scenario stations: rotate through burn, fracture, and anaphylaxis scenarios — apply correct treatment for each
exercises: State the 3 steps for treating a burn
When should you administer a second EpiPen?
What signs indicate anaphylaxis?
lessons.homework: Research the most common causes of anaphylaxis and design a prevention poster for a school canteen.

revision.notes: Burns: 20 min cool water + cover + call 999. Fracture: support + don't move. Anaphylaxis: EpiPen + 999.
revision.tip: Never remove clothing stuck to a burn — cool the burn through clothing if necessary.

lessons.assessment: Respond to three written emergency scenarios (burn, fracture, anaphylaxis) — give the correct step-by-step treatment for each.

lessons.title: Thermal Physics
lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.reading_material: All matter is made of particles in constant motion. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles. Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Q = mcΔT.
practical_activities: Compare heating rates of water and oil
Calculate energy needed to heat water to boiling point
exercises: Calculate Q when 2 kg of water rises 20°C (c=4200 J/kg°C)
Explain why cooking pots have metal bases but plastic handles
lessons.homework: Investigate the specific heat capacity of aluminium using a known method.

revision.notes: Q = mcΔT — energy = mass × specific heat × temperature change.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the specific heat capacity of water in J/kg°C?
What does Q = mcΔT calculate?

lessons.assessment: Calculation: Solve 5 Q = mcΔT problems with different substances.

lessons.title: Space Physics
lessons.subject: Physics
learning_objectives: Describe the life cycle of a star
Describe evidence for an expanding universe
lessons.reading_material: Stars form from nebulae, live as main sequence stars, then evolve into red giants, and end as white dwarfs (small stars) or supernovae/neutron stars/black holes (massive stars). The Big Bang theory states the universe began ~13.8 billion years ago.
practical_activities: Research the life cycle of the Sun
Analyse galaxy redshift data
exercises: Trace the life cycle of a star 10x the mass of our Sun
Explain two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang
lessons.homework: Create a poster showing the life cycle of a massive star compared to our Sun.

revision.notes: Red giants → low mass stars → white dwarfs. Massive stars → supernovae → neutron stars or black holes.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the main evidence that the universe is expanding?
What will eventually happen to our Sun?

lessons.assessment: Essay: Describe the life cycle of a star and explain two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.

lessons.title: Electrochemistry
lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.reading_material: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to split ionic compounds. At the cathode (-): cations gain electrons (reduction). At the anode (+): anions lose electrons (oxidation). Key uses: electroplating, purifying copper, producing aluminium.
practical_activities: Electrolyse copper sulfate solution (teacher demonstration)
Observe products and relate to theory
exercises: Write half equations for Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Predict products from aqueous sodium chloride electrolysis
lessons.homework: Explain why copper is used in electrical wiring and how it is purified by electrolysis.

revision.notes: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: At which electrode does reduction occur?
What is produced at the cathode during electrolysis of copper sulfate?

lessons.assessment: Half-equation questions: Write and balance half equations for 4 electrode reactions.

lessons.title: Rates of Reaction and Equilibrium
lessons.subject: Chemistry
learning_objectives: Explain dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
lessons.reading_material: Reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy. Rate increases with: temperature, concentration, surface area, pressure (for gases), catalysts. At equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
practical_activities: Investigate effect of temperature on rate of reaction (e.g., sodium thiosulfate + HCl)
Graph results
exercises: Explain why increasing concentration increases rate
State Le Chatelier's principle and apply to one example
lessons.homework: Explain why food is stored in a refrigerator using collision theory.

revision.notes: Le Chatelier: if you stress a system at equilibrium, it shifts to relieve that stress.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which factor does NOT increase rate of reaction?
What happens when temperature increases in an exothermic reversible reaction at equilibrium?

lessons.assessment: Data analysis: Describe and explain the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction from given data.

lessons.title: Evolution and Natural Selection
lessons.subject: Biology
learning_objectives: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection
lessons.reading_material: Charles Darwin proposed that organisms best adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — natural selection. Over many generations this leads to evolution of species.
practical_activities: Analyse case studies: peppered moth, antibiotic resistance
Create an adaptation profile for an animal
exercises: List 4 pieces of evidence for evolution
Explain how antibiotic resistance develops
lessons.homework: Research one example of observable evolution and present your findings.

revision.notes: Evolution is change in allele frequency in a population over time — NOT change in an individual.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is natural selection?
options: Survival and reproduction of best-adapted individuals
questions.correct: Survival and reproduction of best-adapted individuals

questions.question: Which is NOT evidence for evolution?

lessons.assessment: Case study report: Explain how antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example of natural selection.

lessons.title: Human Reproduction and Development
lessons.subject: Biology
learning_objectives: Describe the male and female reproductive systems
Understand puberty and the menstrual cycle
lessons.reading_material: Human reproduction is sexual. Sperm cells fertilise egg cells in the fallopian tube, forming a zygote that develops into an embryo. The menstrual cycle prepares the uterus for pregnancy each month.
practical_activities: Model the menstrual cycle using a timeline
Calculate the fertile window from a cycle chart
exercises: Label diagrams of the male and female reproductive system
Describe the role of the placenta
lessons.homework: Write a fact sheet explaining puberty changes for a Grade 5 student.

revision.notes: The menstrual cycle is about 28 days. Ovulation occurs at approximately day 14.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually occur?
What is the role of the placenta?
options: Exchanges nutrients and waste between mother and foetus
questions.correct: Exchanges nutrients and waste between mother and foetus

lessons.assessment: Short answer: Describe the changes that occur during puberty in males and females.

lessons.title: Philosophy of Mind and Free Will
lessons.subject: Philosophy
learning_objectives: Define consciousness and the mind-body problem
lessons.reading_material: The philosophy of mind asks: what is consciousness? The mind-body problem: how does the mental relate to the physical? Dualism (Descartes) says mind and body are separate substances. Physicalism says the mind is nothing over and above the brain. Free will: do we freely choose our actions? Hard determinism says all events (including our choices) are caused by prior events — no free will. Libertarianism (philosophical) says genuine free will exists. Compatibilism argues free will and determinism can both be true.
practical_activities: Thought experiment: if scientists could predict every choice you'd ever make, would you still have free will? Debate in groups
exercises: Explain Descartes' mind-body dualism
What is the difference between hard determinism and compatibilism?
Give one argument for and one against free will
lessons.homework: Read a short summary of Daniel Dennett's compatibilist position and write your reaction (150 words).

revision.notes: Dualism = mind and body separate. Physicalism = mind is brain. Compatibilism = free will + determinism can coexist.
revision.tip: Free will debates connect to law, morality, and responsibility — think about practical implications.

quiz.question: Physicalism claims
options: Mind is identical to or depends on the brain
quiz.correct: Mind is identical to or depends on the brain

quiz.question: Compatibilism holds that
options: Free will and determinism are contradictory
Free will and determinism can both be true
quiz.correct: Free will and determinism can both be true

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word essay arguing either for or against the existence of free will.
textbook_references: Oxford A Level Philosophy — Oxford University Press

lessons.title: Problem Solving and Decision Making
lessons.subject: Critical Thinking
lessons.reading_material: Critical thinking culminates in structured problem solving. The scientific approach: (1) Define the problem clearly; (2) Gather relevant information; (3) Generate possible solutions; (4) Evaluate each solution using criteria; (5) Choose the best option; (6) Reflect on the outcome. Decision matrices help compare options against weighted criteria. Real-world decisions involve trade-offs, uncertainty, and ethical considerations.
practical_activities: Group task: use a decision matrix to choose the best fundraising idea for your school
exercises: List the six steps of structured problem solving
Create a decision matrix comparing three smartphone models
Why should ethical considerations be part of decision making?
lessons.homework: Apply the six-step problem-solving process to a real problem in your school or community.

revision.notes: Problem solving: Define → Gather → Generate → Evaluate → Choose → Reflect.
revision.tip: Weight your criteria by importance before scoring options in a matrix.

quiz.question: The FIRST step in structured problem solving is
A trade-off means
options: Gaining one thing by giving up another
quiz.correct: Gaining one thing by giving up another

lessons.assessment: Write a structured 300-word decision report recommending the best solution to a given dilemma.
textbook_references: Cambridge Thinking Skills — Cambridge University Press

lessons.title: Ethics, Justice, and the Future of Democracy
lessons.subject: Civics
lessons.reading_material: Justice theories: Rawls (fairness from behind 'veil of ignorance'), utilitarianism (greatest good), virtue ethics (character). Democracy faces 21st century challenges: populism, democratic backsliding, disinformation, algorithmic influence, inequality. How do we build more just societies? Active citizenship, constitutional protections, and civic education matter.
practical_activities: Apply Rawls' veil of ignorance to a real policy
Debate: is democracy in decline?

options: Designing society without knowing your position in it
exercises.answer: Designing society without knowing your position in it

homework.task: Write an essay: what is the most important reform to strengthen democracy in your country?

revision.notes: Justice has multiple theories. Democracy needs active citizens and strong institutions.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

options: Erosion of democratic norms and institutions
questions.answer: Erosion of democratic norms and institutions

lessons.title: Sexual and Reproductive Health
lessons.subject: Health Education
learning_objectives: Make informed decisions about relationships and health
lessons.reading_material: Puberty brings physical and emotional changes in adolescence. Reproductive health involves making informed, responsible decisions. Healthy relationships are based on respect, consent, and equality. Contraception and STI prevention are part of responsible sexual health. Seek healthcare providers for personal health questions. Body autonomy: you control your body.

quiz_bank.question: What are exports?

lessons.title: Business Strategy and Growth
lessons.subject: Business Studies
learning_objectives: Apply SWOT analysis to a real business
lessons.reading_material: A business strategy is a long-term plan to achieve goals. Businesses grow organically (by expanding sales and opening new locations) or inorganically (through mergers and acquisitions). A SWOT analysis identifies Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. Globalisation means businesses now compete internationally, requiring strategies adapted to different markets. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is increasingly important in modern strategy.
practical_activities: Conduct a SWOT analysis for a local school canteen — present findings to the class
exercises: Distinguish organic from inorganic growth with an example each
What are the risks of a merger?
Explain why CSR is becoming more important for large businesses
lessons.homework: Choose a well-known company and write a one-page SWOT analysis using news articles and the company website.

revision.notes: SWOT = Strengths, Weaknesses (internal); Opportunities, Threats (external). Organic = self-grown; Inorganic = takeovers.
revision.tip: Read business news regularly — real SWOT examples are everywhere.

quiz.question: A merger involves
options: Two companies joining to form one
quiz.correct: Two companies joining to form one

quiz.question: Which is an EXTERNAL factor in SWOT?

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word strategy recommendation for a business facing declining sales.

lessons.title: Global Power Shifts
lessons.subject: World Politics
learning_objectives: Analyse the concept of unipolarity and multipolarity
Evaluate the rise of new powers (China, India, EU)
Assess the impact of non-state actors on global order
lessons.reading_material: The post-Cold War 'unipolar moment' (USA as sole superpower) is giving way to a multipolar world where multiple centres of power coexist. China's GDP has overtaken the USA in purchasing power parity. India is projected to be the third largest economy by 2030. The EU exercises collective power through trade and regulation. Non-state actors — MNCs, NGOs, terrorist organisations, and social media platforms — increasingly shape global politics. The UN system faces challenges from great power rivalry and new threats (cyber, climate, pandemics).
practical_activities: Debate: 'China will surpass the USA as the dominant global power by 2050' — prepare and argue assigned position
exercises: Define unipolarity and multipolarity with examples
Give two examples of non-state actors and explain their global influence
What is the difference between soft power and hard power?
lessons.homework: Research China's Belt and Road Initiative — what countries are involved and what are the geopolitical implications?

revision.notes: Multipolarity = multiple powerful states. Non-state actors increasingly shape politics. Soft power = influence; hard power = military/economic coercion.
revision.tip: Global power is about more than military — economy, culture, and technology all count.

quiz.question: 'Soft power' refers to
options: Influence through culture, values, and diplomacy
quiz.correct: Influence through culture, values, and diplomacy

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word analysis: Is the world becoming more or less stable as it moves from unipolarity to multipolarity?
textbook_references: Oxford International Relations for A Level

learning_objectives: Analyse real-world problems using CS concepts
lessons.reading_material: Computational thinking: decomposition (break into parts), abstraction (focus on essentials), pattern recognition, algorithms. Binary: computers use 0s and 1s.
